name: Militarism
summary: Militarism holds that war is a permanent and even ennobling feature of relations between states, that a state's highest end is power, and that the armed forces and martial virtues (obedience, duty, self-sacrifice) deserve primacy in state and society. Its classical theorists rejected arbitration, disarmament and the peace movement, defended conquest and colonies as the right of the stronger, and wanted universal service, a military-minded education and a government or monarch above parliamentary politics. Scholars such as Vagts distinguish it from the ordinary 'military way' of preparing for war under civilian direction.
scope: Classical militarism as a doctrine of state and society: Wilhelmine German writers (Treitschke's Politics lectures, Moltke's 1880 letter to Bluntschli, Bernhardi's Germany and the Next War, Ludendorff's Der totale Krieg), Imperial Japanese militarism (the 1882 Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors and the Kodo-faction programme as documented by the IMTFE), with North Korea's Songun as the main modern case, framed by Vagts, the Gale and Kamman encyclopedia entries and Michael Mann. It excludes ordinary support for national defence and the Nazi variant, whose racial programme goes beyond militarism. Where these strands split (religion, economic system, race, one-party rule) the answer is 0 or low; on most social and economic questions militarism has no doctrine and answers are low.

keyFigures.name: Friedrich von Bernhardi
keyFigures.role: Prussian general whose Germany and the Next War (1912) is the classic statement of militarist doctrine

keyFigures.name: Heinrich von Treitschke
keyFigures.role: Historian whose lectures on politics defined the state as power and praised war

keyFigures.name: Erich Ludendorff
keyFigures.role: General who ran Germany's war effort in 1916-18 and theorised total war

sources.title: Germany and the Next War
sources.author: Friedrich von Bernhardi (trans. Allen H. Powles, 1914)
sources.usedFor: War as biological necessity, rejection of arbitration and peace as policy aim, right of conquest, colonies, state as power, universal service, national education, Reichstag and parliamentary government, social policy and social democracy, international law.

sources.title: Selections from Treitschke's Lectures on Politics
sources.author: Heinrich von Treitschke (trans. Adam L. Gowans, 1914)
sources.usedFor: State as the power of offence and defence, obedience without consent, war as permanent and as moulder of nations, weak nations, colonies, monarchy and hereditary succession, women, Jews, Manchesterism.

sources.title: Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors (1882)
sources.author: Emperor Meiji (English translation, Nippon Rikukaigun)
sources.usedFor: Emperor's undelegated supreme command, loyalty, obedience, duty over life, soldiers kept out of politics.

sources.title: The 'Total' War: General Ludendorff's Der totale Krieg, with extracts
sources.author: Erich Ludendorff (digest with translated extracts, Friends of Europe pamphlet no. 36, 1936)
sources.usedFor: Total war and total politics, commander-in-chief's final authority, economic self-sufficiency, family and birth rate, spiritual solidarity, anti-Christian and antisemitic strand.

sources.title: Moltke's letter to Bluntschli, December 1880 (quoted in Shabtai Rosenne's address, ZaöRV 1987)
sources.author: Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, quoted by Shabtai Rosenne
sources.usedFor: Perpetual peace a dream, war part of God's world order, war unfolds the noblest virtues and prevents materialism.

sources.title: Judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, Chapter IV: The Military Domination of Japan and Preparations for War
sources.author: IMTFE (HyperWar edition)
sources.usedFor: Kodo and Hakko Ichiu doctrine, Araki's Kodo faction, Hashimoto's call to destroy parties and the Diet, military training in schools, censorship, controlled economy.

sources.title: Military-First Politics (Songun): Understanding Kim Jong-il's North Korea
sources.author: Han S. Park (Korea Economic Institute Academic Paper Series, 2007)
sources.usedFor: Songun principles: devotion to the leader, defence industry as core of the economy, military education in schools, family rewards, nuclear programme.

sources.title: North Korea's Military-First Policy: A Curse or a Blessing?
sources.author: Alexander Vorontsov (Brookings Institution, 2006)
sources.usedFor: Songun replacing the party and proletariat with the army as society's driving force; the army's economic role.

sources.title: Militarism (Encyclopedia of American Foreign Policy; International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences)
sources.author: William Kamman; Gale encyclopedia entry (via Encyclopedia.com)
sources.usedFor: Definition (values war, primacy of armed forces), Vagts's distinction from the military way, ideal-type cases in Japan 1931-45 and Germany 1916-18, officer aristocracy, militarism in democracies, imperialism.

sources.title: The Roots and Contradictions of Modern Militarism
sources.author: Michael Mann (New Left Review I/162, 1987)
sources.usedFor: Definition of militarism as treating war and its preparation as normal and desirable; deterrence-science militarism tied to industrial technology (opening sections only; rest paywalled).

missingStatements.text: International disputes should be settled by binding arbitration rather than by war.
missingStatements.rationale: Bernhardi devotes a chapter to arguing that arbitration treaties are futile and harmful to a rising nation, and Moltke dismissed codified peace as a dream.
missingStatements.declined: Statement bank frozen on 2026-10-22, before the people audits: no new statements are added.

missingStatements.text: War is a permanent feature of relations between states that can never be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: Treitschke says war will last as long as there is more than one state, and Moltke calls perpetual peace a dream.

notes: Strands split on religion (Bernhardi and Moltke Christian, Ludendorff anti-Christian, Japan state Shinto, Songun secular), on the economic system (private Wilhelmine and Japanese economies versus Songun's planned one) and on race (Ludendorff and Treitschke antisemitic, others not); those answers are 0 or low. The Kokutai no Hongi and Vagts's and Berghahn's books could not be read in full online (copyright-restricted), so Vagts is cited through the encyclopedia entries. The 1882 Rescript tells soldiers to stay out of politics, in tension with later Japanese officers' political role.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Bernhardi praises the Imperial state's sickness, accident and old-age insurance as binding workers to the nation, but militarism as such has no health policy.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Militarists put military needs above market allocation, as Ludendorff and Songun show, but they do not reject markets in principle.

public-ownership.rationale: Songun North Korea owns industry publicly while Prussian and Japanese militarism worked with private firms, so strands are split.

cut-welfare.rationale: Bernhardi defends Imperial social legislation as the state's duty and a remedy for revolutionary agitation, a view other militarists did not stress.

strong-leader.rationale: Ludendorff demands that in total war the commander's decision be final in every sphere of life, and Bernhardi praises a government above all parties; a leader free of parliamentary gridlock is the ideal.

state-harmful.rationale: Treitschke defines the state as the public power of offence and defence and writes that without war there would be no state, so the state is the precondition of everything militarists value.

empower-police-military.rationale: Bernhardi's book is a sustained demand that Germany enlarge its army and navy and that the whole nation fund them; the Gale definition makes primacy of the armed forces in state and society the mark of militarism.

traditional-family.rationale: Ludendorff wants large healthy families to supply the army, Songun rewards families that send children to serve, and Treitschke defends the patriarchal family.

more-religion-public.rationale: Strands are split: Bernhardi calls Christianity combative and valuable, Ludendorff wants Christianity purged, and Japanese militarism leaned on state Shinto.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Bernhardi treats German culture as a world mission that military power must protect and spread.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Bernhardi calls arbitration courts and peace treaties futile and harmful to a rising nation, and Treitschke says no judge above sovereign states can even be imagined.

free-trade.rationale: Treitschke ridicules the Manchester view of man as a being who buys cheap and sells dear, and Bernhardi sees trade rivalry as a cause of war rather than of harmony.

nation-first.rationale: Bernhardi writes that the end-all and be-all of a state is power, and Treitschke that the state's first duty is to maintain itself; neither admits a duty of global cooperation above national interest.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Militarists favour using force abroad, but for national power rather than human rights; Treitschke's civilizing sword is the closest they come, so the answer is neutral.

revolution-justified.rationale: Bernhardi says Imperial social legislation removed any excuse for revolutionary agitation, though Japanese militarist officers attempted coups, so the picture is mixed.

central-planning.rationale: Strands are split: Songun runs a planned economy, Ludendorff wanted wartime controls, and Wilhelmine militarists accepted a private economy.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Ludendorff calls for coordinating industry and agriculture to serve military needs, and Songun makes the defence industry the core of the economy.

one-party-rule.rationale: Hashimoto wanted a single Army party and Songun operates in a one-party state, but Prussian militarism worked within a multiparty Reich, so strands are split.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

reviewHistory.rationale: Treitschke's lectures argue the monarchy is the best form and want the Hohenzollern kingship kept strong; the Rescript makes the Emperor supreme commander for all time.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

democracy-best.rationale: Bernhardi, Treitschke and Japan's militarist officers rejected parliamentary democracy for their nations, but the Gale entry notes militarism also exists inside democracies, so the stance is disagreement rather than total rejection.

right-to-secede.rationale: Treitschke recalls that Prussia's claim to lead Germany was proved on the battlefield against the small states; the unity won by arms is not up for secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Treitschke argues a monarch sees further than ordinary men, and Kamman notes the officer aristocracy prized hierarchy and rank.

political-violence-never.rationale: Militarists treat force as the final arbiter of political claims; Treitschke calls war the decisive proof among states, and Japanese militarist officers backed assassinations and coups (IMTFE).

war-builds-character.rationale: Moltke wrote that perpetual peace is a dream and that war unfolds the noblest human virtues; Treitschke calls war the mightiest moulder of nations, and Bernhardi calls it a biological necessity for national vigour.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: No militarist text bases law on scripture; Bernhardi says Christian ethics cannot govern the state and Ludendorff rejects Christianity.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Treitschke defines the state as the public power of offence and defence, so defence by private firms contradicts the militarist idea of the state.

military-superiority.rationale: Bernhardi argues Germany must build forces able to defeat its rivals rather than merely deter them, since peace cannot be the goal of policy; maintaining a strong military is the core of the reference definition.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Ludendorff wants an ethnically unified people while Treitschke accepts assimilated Jews as Germans; militarism itself centres on the state, not ethnicity.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Bernhardi and Treitschke see history as driven by the rivalry and wars of states, and Bernhardi wants the working class won back to state and nation.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Bernhardi and Treitschke defend colonial conquest as the right of stronger, higher civilizations, which rules out any debt to the colonized.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Bernhardi and the Rescript prize self-sacrifice for the state and treat private interest as subordinate, though they do not condemn honest gain.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Bernhardi says that in war the individual disappears before the conception of the state and must sacrifice himself; the Rescript tells soldiers duty is heavier than a mountain and death lighter than a feather.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Modern militarism depends on industry, as Ludendorff's total war and Mann's military science show, so it does not reject industrial civilization, though it never discusses the claim.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Militarist writers treat war as permanent in a world of states and part of the order of things (Treitschke, Moltke); Ludendorff blamed hostile supranational powers, not capitalism.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Bernhardi makes the nation and state the bearer of right and duty, and Songun teaching says individuals exist only for the organized collective.

conscription.rationale: Bernhardi praises universal military service as a school of the nation and wants it fully applied; the Meiji Rescript rests on the restored conscript army, and Songun sets ten-year service.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Ludendorff stresses racial inheritance, but Bernhardi, the Rescript and Songun texts are about nations and states, not genetic ability; strands are split.

total-state.rationale: Ludendorff calls for a total politics that mobilizes economy, people and spirit for war, and Songun makes the army the organizing core of economy and education; older Prussian writers stopped short of directing all culture.

national-rebirth.rationale: Japan's militarists sought a Showa restoration to purge party politics, and Ludendorff hailed a racial awakening after the war; renewal of martial spirit is a recurring theme.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Bernhardi holds that growing nations need new territory and that the victor, not the possessor, has the right; Treitschke writes that states expand mostly by conquest.

universal-morality.rationale: Bernhardi argues Christian morality is personal and cannot govern states, and that each nation has its own conception of right.

national-self-determination.rationale: Treitschke says weak nations rightly perish and Bernhardi that the victor has the right, so no nation has a right to its own state merely by being a nation.

force-without-un.rationale: Bernhardi rejects arbitration and any outside authority over a nation's decision for war, so approval by an international body is not needed.

class-collaboration.rationale: Bernhardi wants workers reconciled with the existing state through social legislation, and Ludendorff makes the solidarity of the whole people the foundation of total war.

workers-nation.rationale: Bernhardi attacks international social democracy as hostile to the national state and wants workers won back to the ideals of country.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Treitschke writes that history wears masculine features and is not for women, and attacks the emancipation of women.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Ludendorff calls oil and motor power an iron necessity for war; expanding domestic production follows from that, though he does not say so.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Treitschke wanted Jews treated as guests rather than full members, and Bernhardi ranks nations; equal legal standing for all is not a militarist value, though the texts focus on nations.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Treitschke writes that citizens' inward consent is not absolutely necessary and that kingdoms have lasted for centuries without it.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Bernhardi defends aggressive war and conquest when national interest demands it, and Treitschke calls war the form of lawsuit by which states enforce their claims.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Bernhardi presents the struggle for existence as a law of nature that war carries into the life of nations; Treitschke says brave nations thrive and weak ones rightly go to the wall.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Bernhardi wants willing workers protected against social democratic tyranny, that is, against union and party pressure on workers.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Ludendorff wants corrupt and disloyal elements treated ruthlessly in total war, and Japan's military-led governments expanded police control of opinion; ordinary protections yield to wartime unity.

party-controls-media.rationale: Bernhardi wants the government to use the press for national enlightenment, and Japan's militarist regime censored the media, but neither calls for party ownership of media.

party-commands-army.rationale: In Imperial Japan the army answered to the Emperor, not a party, and Songun lifted the army and the leader's defence commission above the party; militarists resist party control of the forces.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Treitschke calls the dream of a world state irrational and treats sovereignty, the power to declare war when it chooses, as essential to a state.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The Rescript says supreme command stays in the Emperor's hands and is never delegated to a subject; Ludendorff insists the commander-in-chief must have undisputed control with no parliamentary interference.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Bernhardi and Ludendorff blame internationalist agitation for weakening the nation, and Ludendorff demands total solidarity behind the army in war.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Bernhardi treats alliances as useful instruments and wants troops ready abroad, though he stresses self-reliance over allies.

people-in-arms.rationale: Bernhardi wants universal service built around a trained standing army and officer corps, and Kamman notes the officer caste's central place; a militia replacing the professional army was a liberal and socialist demand.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Treitschke celebrates German unification by war and Songun claims Korean reunification, though neither frames it as a general rule.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Bernhardi calls Germany the greatest civilized people in history, and Treitschke says weak and cowardly nations go to the wall and rightly so.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Bernhardi holds that territory belongs to the victor and opposes peace bought by concessions, but militarism is not tied to a historic homeland.

collective-defense.rationale: Bernhardi accepts alliance obligations when they serve German power, but treats them as instruments, not principles.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Bernhardi states that in the clash of nations it is not the possessor but the victor who has the right, so conquest settles title.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Bernhardi praises a German government that stands above all parties, and Treitschke prizes the monarchy as the unifying national tradition.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Treitschke praises the wars of German unification as the decisive proof against the small states, and treats force as the state's means of holding itself together.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The Rescript traces the Emperor to Jimmu and Songun all but deifies the leader, but Prussian militarism did not treat the Kaiser as divine.

character-from-environment.rationale: Bernhardi stresses that military service and schooling form character, while Ludendorff stresses racial inheritance, so strands are split.

leader-cult.rationale: Songun binds the army to the leader in life and death, and the Rescript to the Emperor, but Prussian militarism lacked a mass leader cult.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Treitschke sees history made by the wars and rivalry of states, and Moltke prizes war as a check on materialism; economic determinism is foreign to them.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Ludendorff wants Germany as self-sufficient as possible in all commodities for war, and Bernhardi wants protective measures to reduce dependence on enemies.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Treitschke defends hereditary monarchy and Kamman notes the Prussian officer corps drew rank and power from the nobility.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Bernhardi wants national education to teach German greatness and the duty to the state, and Japan's militarist schooling centred on the national polity.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Bernhardi writes that higher civilization and the greater power that goes with it are the foundation of the right to annexation.

patriotic-education.rationale: Bernhardi devotes chapters to national education that should foster a military spirit; Japan put army officers in schools to drill pupils (IMTFE), and Songun makes military training the backbone of the curriculum.

elective-rulers.rationale: Treitschke treats hereditary succession as a condition of monarchy, which he holds the best form of state.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Rescript makes loyalty to the Emperor absolute, and Songun demands soldiers live and die with the leader; a right of subjects to remove the ruler has no place.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Bernhardi writes that no people is so little suited as the Germans to parliamentary or republican government and mocks the Reichstag; Treitschke wants a constitutional monarchy that keeps the kingship strong.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Bernhardi recalls William I's sense of the state's duty to those badly equipped with necessities, a paternalist stance not elaborated elsewhere.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The Gale entry defines militarism as giving the armed forces primacy in state and society, and in Japan and under Songun the military became the dominant political force; but the 1882 Rescript itself told soldiers to keep out of politics.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Bernhardi resents the Reichstag's haggling over military funds and wants the nation's resources made available to the army, though the Imperial system he defends did keep a budget vote.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Moltke wrote that without war the world would sink into materialism, and Treitschke scorns a commercial view of life.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Ludendorff warns that falling births endanger military power and wants large families promoted; Songun gives families of soldiers larger rations.

democratic-peace.rationale: Treitschke says war will last as long as there is more than one state, and Moltke calls perpetual peace a dream; no form of government abolishes war.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Treitschke says the state demands obedience and its laws must be kept whether willingly or not; the Rescript makes obedience the soldier's core virtue.

non-intervention.rationale: Treitschke holds that every sovereign state has the right to declare war when it chooses, and Bernhardi justifies attacking rivals for national interest; a blanket ban on intervention is rejected.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Ludendorff blamed a Jewish and Roman Catholic conspiracy and Treitschke wrote against Jewish influence, but Japanese and Songun militarism lacked this theme, so it is a strand view.

local-production.rationale: Self-sufficiency for war, as Ludendorff urges, favours domestic production, though he does not address local markets.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Bernhardi argues no self-respecting nation would sacrifice its own conception of right to a universal international law.

defeat-communism.rationale: Japanese militarists were anti-communist, but Songun is itself a communist-state doctrine, so strands are split.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Bernhardi calls for vigorous opposition to social democracy, and Japan's militarists crushed parties and censored the press (IMTFE); suppression serves national unity behind the army.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Bernhardi presents colonies as a necessity for German power and growth, and Treitschke wants a colony won in the next successful war; colonies serve the metropole's strength.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Japanese militarism grounded command in the divine Emperor and Moltke saw war in God's order, but Ludendorff rejected Christian authority and Songun is secular, so strands are split.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Treitschke calls protection of citizens by arms the first and essential task of the state; militarism as defined holds that a state must keep strong forces.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Treitschke treats hereditary succession as a condition of real monarchy, and Songun legitimated Kim Jong Il's succession to his father.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Treitschke holds that the state must enforce obedience to its laws whether willingly or not; abolishing coercive institutions is the opposite.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Japan's militarists organized military training in schools and nationalist youth societies, Songun makes military education compulsory, and Bernhardi wants youth prepared for service.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Rescript demands soldiers be ready to die and kill for the throne, and Treitschke praises the moral majesty of war; absolute non-violence is the opposite of militarism.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The Rescript teaches that death for the throne is lighter than a feather, and Songun praises sacrifice beside the leader as the soldier's highest quality.

person-over-state.rationale: Bernhardi subordinates the individual wholly to the state's power and survival, and Songun doctrine as reported by Han Park says individuals are meaningless unless organized for the collective.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Ludendorff calls the spiritual solidarity of a people the foundation of all, and Moltke opposes materialism, but the strands give different religious grounds.

racial-pride.rationale: Ludendorff exalts racial inheritance and Bernhardi German greatness, but most militarist texts speak of the nation rather than race.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Bernhardi rejects the view that only defensive war is legitimate, insisting that the maintenance of peace can never be the goal of policy and that a state may strike first when its interests demand.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Bernhardi describes Germany as encircled by England and France bent on hemming it in, and Songun justifies itself by a hostile encirclement.

arms-reduction.rationale: Bernhardi treats disarmament and peace schemes as harmful to a rising nation and wants armaments expanded; Treitschke scorns the blind worshippers of perpetual peace.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Treitschke defines the state as the public power of offence and defence that must be obeyed, implying it alone commands armed force.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The 1882 Rescript makes obedience to superiors as to the Emperor and duty heavier than a mountain the soldier's creed; Songun's first principle is that the army lives and dies with the leader.

sacred-nation.rationale: Ludendorff calls troops to fight for the immortal people and Bernhardi asks for devotion and self-sacrifice to state and country.

women-suffrage.rationale: Treitschke mocks experiments with female suffrage, but this is his own view; Songun North Korea formally keeps women's suffrage, so militarism as such has no single position.

equal-conscription.rationale: Classical militarists conscripted men only, while North Korea later drafted women, so strands differ.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Treitschke's national power politics supports protecting nationals abroad, though he does not state such a rule.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Militarist writers defend national property and conquest, not a universal common claim on resources, though the question is not raised.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Bernhardi praises broad Imperial social insurance, but militarism has no doctrine on targeting.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Bernhardi wants government and nation to stand above party feeling, and the IMTFE records militarist calls to sweep away the political parties; parties are seen as dividing the nation.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Ludendorff demands strict justice in wartime economic controls, but militarism generally works with favoured arms industries; no clear stand.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Ludendorff wants national solidarity above confessional divisions and Bernhardi wants party feeling merged in national defence, so a nation-first politics over denominations follows loosely.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Japanese militarism joined modern arms to ancestral loyalty, and Ludendorff pairs modern weapons with racial-spiritual revival, though neither states this as a principle.

national-resource-control.rationale: Ludendorff sees command of oil fields as an object of world politics and wants supplies secured, implying national control.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The statement concerns domestic racial disadvantage, which militarism as a doctrine of war and state power does not address; its strands differ on race.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Only the Songun strand has one-party socialist rule and it has no settled view on markets, while the other strands are not socialist; adherents are split.
